guide.title: Borgo, Rome: Castel Sant'Angelo, the Leonine City and the Quarter That Was Demolished
guide.intro: Borgo is Rome's fourteenth rione, the wedge of city between the Tiber and the border of Vatican City. Roma Capitale's Annuario statistico 2022 gives it the toponymic code 114, an area of 0.5 km² and 2,689 residents at the end of 2021; Roma Capitale's own street register, SISTO, records the rione in Municipio I under a council deliberation of 11 March 2013. Italian Wikipedia says Sixtus V constituted it as the fourteenth rione on 9 December 1586, and that its residents are called borghiciani; its main east–west streets are still called borghi rather than vie, and via della Conciliazione is the modern exception. That street is the thing to understand first. What a visitor walks today is not the quarter that stood here in 1935: between 1936 and 1950 the block of houses at the rione's centre was demolished, and a good deal of what this guide describes is what replaced it.

sections.heading: The spina, and the street that replaced it
sections.body: Until 1936 a wedge of houses called the spina stood between two streets, Borgo Vecchio and Borgo Nuovo, running from the Tiber towards St Peter's. Borgo Vecchio replaced the collapsed medieval Portica — Italian Wikipedia cites its near-constant width of 6.90 metres as the evidence — and Borgo Nuovo was the Via Alexandrina, opened by Alexander VI for the Jubilee of 1500. Demolition began ceremonially on 29 October 1936 at 09.00, when Mussolini struck the cornice of Palazzo Sauve in piazza Pia with a pickaxe, accompanied by the governor Giuseppe Bottai; the project had been shown to Mussolini at Castel Sant'Angelo on 20 June 1936 and to Pius XI in the Loggia di Raffaello eight days later. Expropriations ran under Regio Decreto 981 of 1931, and the named contractors were Vaselli, La Prenestina, Tudini e Talenti, Federici and Manfredi. By 8 October 1937 the spina had ceased to exist and St Peter's was visible from Castel Sant'Angelo. Most of the displaced residents were moved to the borgate, among them Acilia, and no survey of the old quarter was ever made — only drawings. Piazza Scossacavalli, the square at the centre of the spina, went in 1937; its fountain by Carlo Maderno was re-erected in front of Sant'Andrea della Valle, in rione Sant'Eustachio, where it still stands. So did San Giacomo a Scossacavalli in 1937, the Oratorio di San Filippo Neri in Borgo in 1938, San Michele Arcangelo ai Corridori and the Ospedale di San Carlo in 1939, Santa Maria della Purità between 1937 and 1940, and Sangallo's Palazzo del Governatore di Borgo in 1936–37. None was rebuilt. Older losses lie under the same ground: the Meta Romuli, a pyramidal Roman tomb in the Ager Vaticanus, was demolished in 1499, and the round tomb beside it known as the Terebinto di Nerone had gone from the seventh century. This account is Italian Wikipedia's, citing Vannelli, Parisi Presicce and Petacco, the Archivio Centrale dello Stato, Ceccarelli and Borgatti.

sections.heading: The Vatican edge
sections.body: Borgo runs up to the border of Vatican City. St Peter's Basilica, St Peter's Square, the Vatican Museums and the Sistine Chapel are inside a sovereign state and belong to no rione. St Peter's Square is Vatican territory under Article 3 of the Lateran Treaty, and the Italian policing carried out there is a concession on foreign soil rather than evidence of Italian territory. Where the line actually runs is not fixed in words: the Treaty fixes it only by an annexed map at 1:5000, with no verbal description at all; the border commission of 1932–33 never had its conclusions ratified; and no source confirms the paving detail commonly described as marking the boundary. Between the two states there is a third legal tier that a visitor walks through without noticing. Under Article 15 of the Treaty, a list of named properties standing on Italian soil — several of them on and around via della Conciliazione — carry the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of diplomatic agents. They are not Vatican territory and they are not foreign soil; anyone visiting them is subject to Italian law. The Holy See states that its extraterritorial properties in Rome, the Seminario Romano Minore excepted, are named in the Holy See's own enumeration, following the Holy See's 1982 accession to the 1972 World Heritage Convention. The Leonine wall does not mark that border: Leo IV walled the quarter between 848 and 852 after the Saracen sack of 846, with Lothar I decreeing and part-financing the work in October 846, and Paul III and Pius IV extended it to 1565. Most of the surviving circuit is now the Vatican's own perimeter, and only a stretch of it stands in Borgo.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Borgo has no metro station inside it. Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione names the Ottaviano station, on metro Line A, as its metro link; the station stands beyond the rione boundary, in Prati. OpenStreetMap's rione and quartiere polygons put Roma San Pietro railway station outside Borgo as well, in Quartiere XIII Aurelio. On the ground the rione has two spines. Via della Conciliazione is the one every visitor uses: about 420 metres of sampietrini between Largo Giovanni XXIII, at the Tiber end, and Piazza Pio XII at the Vatican end, CAP 00193. Under the Janiculum, the Galleria Principe Amedeo di Savoia-Aosta carries road traffic through a single bore of 0.250 km to its portal at Porta Santo Spirito; motorcycles under 125 cc are excluded from it. To steer by, Roma Capitale gives Castel Sant'Angelo's address as Lungotevere Castello 50, and the parish of Santa Maria in Traspontina gives its own visitor entrance as via della Conciliazione 14. This guide publishes no walking times and no distance it has not taken from a source, so work the geography out from the street numbers rather than from an impression.

faq.question: How do I get to Borgo?
faq.answer: Borgo has no metro station inside it. Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione names Ottaviano, on metro Line A, as the rione's metro link; that station stands beyond the rione boundary, in Prati. OpenStreetMap's rione and quartiere polygons put Roma San Pietro railway station outside Borgo as well, in Quartiere XIII Aurelio. Inside the rione the main axis is via della Conciliazione, about 420 metres of sampietrini running between Largo Giovanni XXIII at the Tiber end and Piazza Pio XII at the Vatican end, CAP 00193; under the Janiculum the Galleria Principe Amedeo di Savoia-Aosta brings road traffic to its portal at Porta Santo Spirito, and motorcycles under 125 cc are excluded from it. This guide publishes no walking times, so steer by street numbers: Roma Capitale gives Castel Sant'Angelo's address as Lungotevere Castello 50, and the parish of Santa Maria in Traspontina gives its visitor entrance as via della Conciliazione 14.

faq.question: Is St Peter's Basilica in Borgo?
faq.answer: No. St Peter's Basilica, St Peter's Square, the Vatican Museums and the Sistine Chapel are inside Vatican City, a sovereign state that belongs to no rione. St Peter's Square is Vatican territory under Article 3 of the Lateran Treaty; the Italian policing there is a concession on foreign soil, not evidence of Italian territory.

faq.question: Where exactly does Vatican City begin at the end of via della Conciliazione?
faq.answer: No source states it precisely, and the reason is in the Lateran Treaty itself: the Treaty fixes the border only by an annexed map at 1:5000, with no verbal description, and the border commission of 1932–33 never had its conclusions ratified. No source confirms the strip of paving often described as marking the line.

faq.question: What does it mean that some buildings in Borgo are called extraterritorial?
faq.answer: It is a third legal tier, and it is not the Vatican. Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership of this property (Art. 13; Annex II). Art. 15 states that the property, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is on Italian soil and visitors are subject to Italian law. In Borgo the Holy See's own published enumeration names the Palazzo del Sant'Offizio and its adjacencies, the Palazzo dei Convertendi, the Palazzo delle Congregazioni ai Propilei and the Palazzo Pio, and on the Janiculum the church of Santi Michele e Magno, the Collegio Internazionale S. Monica, the Jesuit Curia Generalizia and the buildings adjoining it on Borgo Santo Spirito.

faq.question: When is Castel Sant'Angelo open?
faq.answer: Roma Capitale states the museum opens Tuesday to Sunday 9.00–19.30, last admission 18.30, closed Mondays, 25 December and 1 January. From 3 August 2026 and for the rest of 2026 it also opens on the first Monday of each month, 14.00–20.00, last admission 19.00, with a 5-euro ticket, no booking and no groups.

faq.question: What happened to the streets in the middle of Borgo?
faq.answer: They were demolished. Between 1936 and 1950 the spina — the wedge of houses between Borgo Vecchio and Borgo Nuovo — was cleared to open via della Conciliazione. Italian Wikipedia records that by 8 October 1937 the spina had ceased to exist and St Peter's was visible from Castel Sant'Angelo, that most of the displaced residents were moved to the borgate, and that no survey of the old quarter was ever made, only drawings.

faq.question: Which churches and museums in Borgo have published hours?
faq.answer: Santa Maria in Traspontina does: its own site lists weekday Eucharistic celebration as 9.00 - 19.00, Sunday and feast-day celebrations at 9.00, 10.30, a 12.30 international Mass and 19.00, and the Rosary daily at 18.15. Roma Capitale gives the Palazzo del Commendatore's courtyard as visitable Monday to Friday 7.30–18.00 and Saturday 7.30–12.00, during the hospital's hours. Santo Spirito in Sassia and the Museo storico nazionale dell'arte sanitaria have no hours here: no source states them, so none are given.

photos.title: Castel Sant'Angelo from the Tiber
photos.description: Castel Sant'Angelo, whose drum is Hadrian's mausoleum, seen across the Tiber with Ponte Sant'Angelo in front of it.
photos.author: Krzysztof Golik

places.name: Castel Sant'Angelo
places.summary: Hadrian's mausoleum, later a fortress and a papal refuge, now a state museum. Roma Capitale's tourism office describes it as monument, archaeological area and museum, and records that it became a museum site in 1925. Roma Capitale states the museum opens Tuesday to Sunday 9.00–19.30, last admission 18.30, closed Mondays, 25 December and 1 January. From 3 August 2026 and for the rest of 2026 it also opens on the first Monday of each month, 14.00–20.00, last admission 19.00, with a 5-euro ticket, no booking and no groups. Tel. 06 6819111.
places.history: Roma Capitale's tourism office gives the address as Lungotevere Castello 50. This guide publishes no construction date for the castle: the datings that circulate are aggregator-only, with no primary source behind them. Italian Wikipedia gives ownership to the Italian State, through the Ministero della cultura, managed since December 2019 by the Direzione Musei statali di Roma. One warning about Roma Capitale's own material: its Castel Sant'Angelo page attributes the Landsknechte of the 1527 Sack of Rome to Charles VIII, while its Porta Santo Spirito page attributes them to Charles V. Charles VIII died in 1498. This guide follows the Porta Santo Spirito page.

places.name: Passetto di Borgo
places.summary: A raised, fortified corridor running along the top of a stretch of wall between the Apostolic Palace and Castel Sant'Angelo. What this guide describes is only the stretch that physically stands in Borgo: the wall above Borgo Sant'Angelo and Borgo Pio, up to its junction with the castle.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia dates the corridor's formation to 1277, under Nicholas III, inside a stretch of the Vatican walls, and records its use as an escape route by Alexander VI in 1494 and by Clement VII in 1527. Roma Capitale's Castel Sant'Angelo page describes it as a raised, fortified passage connecting the Vatican with Castel Sant'Angelo, running over the Vatican walls. The corridor's western end lies inside Vatican City. No source states where along its length the border crosses: the Lateran Treaty fixes the border only by an annexed map at 1:5000, with no verbal description at all, and the border commission of 1932–33 never had its conclusions ratified. No source states its length either, and none states any visiting arrangement.

places.name: Via della Conciliazione
places.summary: The street running about 420 metres from Largo Giovanni XXIII, at the Tiber end, to Piazza Pio XII at the Vatican end. CAP 00193, paved in sampietrini, lined with two rows of obelisk lampposts.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia credits the design to Marcello Piacentini and Attilio Spaccarelli, dates construction from 1936 on the demolition of the Spina di Borgo, and records that the street was completed for the Jubilee of 1950. It is named for the Lateran Pacts of 11 February 1929. The same article, citing Leonardo Benevolo, calls it «una delle opere urbanistiche più discusse e aspramente criticate del Novecento» — which it translates as widely discussed and criticised town planning of the twentieth century — and adds that Benevolo, Cederna, Vannelli and Insolera are all severely critical of it. That is attributed criticism and not this guide's verdict. Largo Giovanni XXIII, at the river end, is given as the street's inizio and carries no separate record here. Palazzo Rusticucci-Accoramboni, built for cardinal Girolamo Rusticucci by Domenico Fontana and Carlo Maderno, was demolished and rebuilt on the street in 1940 by Clemente Busiri Vici; before that it faced piazza Rusticucci, which was itself destroyed in the 1930s.

places.name: Piazza Pio XII
places.summary: The terminal square of via della Conciliazione, formed between Piacentini's two propylaea. Italian Wikipedia records that it occupies roughly the site of the demolished piazza Rusticucci.
places.history: Beyond the square the ground is Vatican City. No source states precisely where that change happens: the Lateran Treaty describes its border only by an annexed 1:5000 map, and the 1932–33 border commission's conclusions were never ratified.

places.name: Auditorium Conciliazione
places.summary: A hall for dance, music, visual arts and congresses, with a foyer, the Chorus Cafè and the Visionarea Art Space gallery, in its own description. Tel. 06 684391.
places.history: The auditorium occupies rooms inside Palazzo San Pio X. The Holy See's own published enumeration of its extraterritorial properties lists «il Palazzo Pio, dichiarato extraterritoriale nel 1979 (con esclusione tuttavia dei locali che ospitano attualmente l'Auditorium)»: the palace holds extraterritorial status and the rooms housing the Auditorium are explicitly excluded from it. The venue's own contacts page gives its box office as a TicketOne outlet at via della Conciliazione 4 and states that the outlet is closed until further notice, with tickets available online or at other authorised sellers and a same-evening box office opening one hour before the performance. Roma Capitale's record for the venue carries no hours and refers visitors to the venue's own site.

places.name: Palazzo San Pio X
places.summary: A modernist block built 1948–1950 by Marcello Piacentini and Giorgio Calza Bini, holding Curia offices and the embassies to the Holy See of Canada and Taiwan. It is frequently miscalled Palazzo Pio XII.
places.history: Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership of this property (Art. 13; Annex II). Art. 15 states that the property, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is on Italian soil and visitors are subject to Italian law. The Holy See's enumeration names it as «il Palazzo Pio, dichiarato extraterritoriale nel 1979 … in sostituzione del Palazzo della Dataria», and excludes from that status the rooms that house the Auditorium Conciliazione. This guide publishes no compass directions for the building: Italian Wikipedia's article contradicts itself about which side of it faces what.

places.name: Palazzo dell'Azione Cattolica
places.summary: A modernist palace of 1948–1950 by Marcello Piacentini and Giorgio Calza Bini, the seat of Azione Cattolica since 1948; Italian Wikipedia records that it also houses diplomatic missions to the Holy See.
places.history: It faces Palazzo San Pio X at the head of the street and shares a block with Santa Maria Annunziata in Borgo. The Holy See's own published enumeration does not name it, this guide follows the Holy See's list, and no extraterritorial status is stated here.

places.name: Palazzo delle Congregazioni ai Propilei
places.summary: Twin modernist buildings flanking the end of via della Conciliazione, built at the end of the 1930s alongside the design of the street and named for their position by the colonnade's propylaea. Italian Wikipedia puts the dicasteries for the causes of saints, divine worship, legislative texts and bishops in the Edificio Nord at number 10, and those for clergy, institutes of consecrated life and culture in the Edificio Sud at number 3, which also holds the Holy See Press Office, entrance at via della Conciliazione 54.
places.history: Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership of this property (Art. 13; Annex II). Art. 15 states that the property, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is on Italian soil and visitors are subject to Italian law. The Holy See's enumeration names it as «il Palazzo delle Congregazioni ai Propilei». One piece of noise to disregard: Italian Wikipedia's infobox for the building carries both an Italian and a Vatican country field. That is an editing artefact, not a sovereignty claim — the Holy See's own list treats the building as an extraterritorial property standing on Italian soil.

places.name: Palazzo dei Convertendi
places.summary: Sixteenth-century in origin, demolished for via della Conciliazione and rebuilt in 1940 on the other side of the new street. Italian Wikipedia gives it as the seat of the Congregation for the Eastern Churches, and it is also called Palazzo della Congregazione per le Chiese orientali.
places.history: Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership of this property (Art. 13; Annex II). Art. 15 states that the property, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is on Italian soil and visitors are subject to Italian law. The Holy See's enumeration names it as «il Palazzo dei Convertendi, sede della Congregazione per le Chiese Orientali». Via dell'Erba separates it from Palazzo Castellesi, and Palazzo Rusticucci-Accoramboni stands on its other flank. The rebuilt palace absorbed what was left of Palazzo Caprini, the house on the edge of piazza Scossacavalli that was sold in 1500 to the apostolic protonotary Adriano Caprini and rebuilt by Bramante; Raphael bought it in 1517 and spent his last three years there. Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione records that the 1937 demolition of the Convertendi exposed vaulted structures belonging to Palazzo Caprini. Its article on via della Conciliazione runs the two buildings together; this guide keeps them apart.

places.name: Palazzo Castellesi (Giraud, Torlonia)
places.summary: A palace built 1499–1517 for cardinal Adriano Castellesi of Corneto. Italian Wikipedia gives its present owners as the Torlonia del Fucino family and its use as a private residence.
places.history: The design is generally attributed to Bramante, and Italian Wikipedia hedges that attribution rather than asserting it; this guide keeps the hedge. The same article describes the façade as rereading Alberti's Palazzo Rucellai by way of the Palazzo della Cancelleria, with twin pilaster orders over smooth travertine ashlar, and the central courtyard as porticoed on all four sides on rectangular piers. The building served in turn as the English embassy, an ecclesiastical college and a hospice, and was known afterwards as Palazzo Giraud and then Palazzo Torlonia. It originally faced piazza Scossacavalli; the demolition of the spina left its façade standing on the edge of via della Conciliazione.

places.name: Palazzo Cesi-Armellini
places.summary: A palace on via della Conciliazione, first built about 1520 for cardinal Francesco Armellini and rebuilt into its present form for cardinal Pier Donato Cesi by Martino Longhi il Vecchio. Italian Wikipedia gives its owner as the general curia of the Society of the Divine Saviour.
places.history: The Cesi family bought the palace in 1565. Italian Wikipedia dates Longhi's rebuilding to 1570–1575 in the body of its article and to 1570–1588 in its infobox; the two do not agree and this guide states both rather than choosing. The same article records that the Landsknechte of Charles V entered Rome through this building in the Sack of 1527. Cutting via della Conciliazione mutilated it: the façade lost five of its thirteen windows, leaving eight, and the monumental staircase was destroyed. Italian Wikipedia describes what stands as a light brick façade in three bands with paired pilasters, an antique lion protome at one corner, a Doric-pilastered portal and a large rectangular courtyard.

places.name: Palazzo Alicorni
places.summary: A sixteenth-century palace built for Trajano Alicorni, restored in 1928, demolished in 1931 and rebuilt in 1938 on a different site.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia records that the Alicorni were an Albanian family who had fled the Ottoman advance under Pius II, and that the palace was demolished in 1931 in the course of defining the boundaries of the new Vatican City State. That is a fact about how a border was made physical on the ground; it is not a statement of where the border runs. Rebuilt in 1938, the palace now faces the Palazzo del Commendatore, with via Scossacavalli separating it from Palazzo dei Penitenzieri and via dell'Ospedale on its other side — a street named for the Ospedale di San Carlo, which was destroyed.

places.name: Palazzo Serristori
places.summary: A palace of 1565 built by Averardo Serristori, ambassador of Cosimo I de' Medici to Pius IV, standing between via della Conciliazione and Borgo Santo Spirito with its main façade on via dei Cavalieri del Santo Sepolcro.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia records that it was built on the site of a small palace owned first by Cesare Borgia and then by cardinal Bartolomeo Della Rovere, and that it became the Tuscan embassy to the pope before that embassy moved to Palazzo Firenze in Campo Marzio. A Renaissance plaque on the building commemorates Serristori. The plain fact worth stating is that this Renaissance palace is still standing, and that the buildings which stood around piazza Scossacavalli are not.

places.name: Palazzo dei Penitenzieri (Palazzo della Rovere)
places.summary: A palace on via della Conciliazione, begun about 1480 for cardinal Domenico Della Rovere. It is owned by the Equestrian Order of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem, which has its Grand Magisterium there.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia gives Baccio Pontelli as a possible architect and records that the palace took its later name under Alexander VII, who moved the penitenzieri confessors into it. The façade is modelled on Palazzo Venezia and carries a corner tower; the central courtyard is on two levels, the upper one kept as a walled garden. A sixteenth-century frescoed gallery runs through the left wing at piano nobile, and the salone in the right wing holds Pinturicchio's Soffitto dei Semidei of 1490; the same article describes the right wing as visitable on request to the Order. In the palace's courtyard, remains identified as the Teatro di Nerone — Nero's private theatre, previously known only from literary sources — were excavated between 2020 and 2023 and announced in 2023, with the Soprintendenza Speciale Archeologia Belle Arti e Paesaggio di Roma as scientific authority. Italian Wikipedia states that the ruins are to be reburied once catalogued, so this guide makes no suggestion that they can be seen.

places.name: Arcispedale di Santo Spirito in Saxia
places.summary: The hospital complex on the river side of Borgo, turned into a hospital by Innocent III in 1198 and now also a conference venue. The working hospital beside it is ASL Roma 1's Presidio S. Spirito in Sassia.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia traces the site to the Schola Saxonum founded by Ine, king of Wessex, at the beginning of the eighth century, and to a xenodochium founded in 794 by Offa of Mercia; Innocent III made it a hospital in 1198, the complex designed by Marchionne Aretino. Its long ward, the Corsia Sistina, was built for Sixtus IV: 120 metres by 12, facing Borgo Santo Spirito, divided under an octagonal tower by a tiburio into the Braccio di sotto and the Braccio di sopra. The altar at the centre of the tiburio is one that, in the source's own hedged phrasing, «dovrebbe essere» a work of Palladio in Rome — the attribution is hedged there and stays hedged here. The portale del Paradiso is attributed to Andrea Bregno, and beside it is the ruota degli esposti, the foundling wheel. A fresco cycle of more than fifty scenes was painted in 1478.

places.name: Palazzo del Commendatore
places.summary: A palace inside the Santo Spirito complex, built 1566–1572 under Pius V to a design by Giovanni Lippi, called Nanni di Baccio Bigio, as the seat of the commendatore of the Ospedali Riuniti di S. Spirito. Roma Capitale states that only the courtyard can be visited, during the opening hours of the ASL Presidio S. Spirito in Sassia: Monday to Friday 7.30–18.00, Saturday 7.30–12.00.
places.history: Roma Capitale describes a two-storey façade of eight windows on each floor, an arcaded courtyard with a seventeenth-century fountain, a loggia at piano nobile and the frescoed Salone del Commendatore, which is booked through the ASL. Set in the courtyard is a nineteenth-century six-hour clock whose single hand is shaped like a lizard, framed by an ouroboros and topped by a bronze cardinal's hat. The same page records that the palace holds the old Spezieria, where medicinal herbs were prepared and whose antique jars and mortars survive, and the Accademia Lancisiana with its library, founded in the eighteenth century under Clement XI.

places.name: Museo storico nazionale dell'arte sanitaria
places.summary: A museum of the history of medicine, surgery and pharmacology, opened in 1933 inside the Santo Spirito complex. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale places the Museo storico nazionale dell'arte sanitaria inside the Palazzo del Commendatore, Borgo Santo Spirito 3. The museum's own site describes its home as the seventeenth-century wing of the Ospedale Santo Spirito in Sassia. Italian Wikipedia gives a Lungotevere in Sassia address and contradicts itself on the number; this guide follows Roma Capitale. The museum's own site records that it was conceived by professors Pietro Capparoni and Giovanni Carbonelli with General Mariano Borgatti and built on the collection of the old Anatomical Museum, and that it documents the passage of medicine, surgery and pharmacology from magic to science. Its holdings include anatomo-pathological preparations and wax models in the sala Flajani, Paolo Mascagni's anatomical plates, and oil paintings that belonged to the anatomist Guglielmo Riva in the sala Alessandrina. Italian Wikipedia adds the institutional chain: an Istituto per il Museo storico dell'Arte Sanitaria founded in 1920 and established by royal decree 1746 of 14 May 1922, which became the Accademia di Storia dell'Arte Sanitaria in 1934, with Santo Spirito granting it a wing in the former corsia Alessandrina in 1929.

places.name: Chiesa di Santo Spirito in Sassia (Santuario della Divina Misericordia)
places.summary: A rectory church beside the Santo Spirito hospital, also the Santuario della Divina Misericordia. Its own site gives the address as Via dei Penitenzieri 12 and the telephone as 06 6879310. No Mass times or opening hours are published here.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia, densely footnoted to Armellini, Hülsen, Krautheimer and Gigli, dates the present church's building to 1538–1590 and its consecration to 17 May 1571, and gives Antonio da Sangallo il Giovane for the church, Baccio Pontelli for the bell tower of about 1471–1475 and Guidetto Guidetti for the façade. It is a rectory rather than a parish and carries a cardinal-deacon's title. The predecessor church of S. Maria in Saxia was founded under Ine with the assent of Gregory II and rebuilt by Leo IV around 850, after the Saracen raid of 846. In 1369 the Byzantine emperor John V Palaiologos abjured the schism here before Urban V.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Maria in Traspontina
places.summary: A Carmelite parish church on via della Conciliazione, which its own site heads BASILICA DI SANTA MARIA IN TRASPONTINA. That site gives the visitor entrance as via della Conciliazione 14, the parish office at Borgo Sant'Angelo 15, the parish priest as p. Giuseppe Midili O.Carm. and the telephone as 06 68806451. Its «Info utili e contatti» block lists weekday Eucharistic celebration as 9.00 - 19.00, Sunday and feast-day celebrations at 9.00, 10.30, a 12.30 international Mass and 19.00, and the Rosary daily at 18.15.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia dates the present church to the sixteenth century and says it replaced an older church that Pius IV had demolished because it blocked the field of fire of Castel Sant'Angelo's guns; that article gives no year for the demolition. For the same defensive reason the dome is very flat and has no drum. The sources do not agree on the architect: the same encyclopedia credits Vignola in its infobox, a Bolognese called Alex Tica in its body text, and G. S. Peruzzi in its article on the rione — three attributions inside one source. The church was built on Borgo Nuovo, so when via della Conciliazione was cut it stayed aligned to the vanished street rather than to the new one, and steps had to be added because the new roadbed sits lower.

places.name: Chiesa di San Lorenzo in Piscibus
places.summary: A twelfth-century church swallowed inside the twentieth-century buildings along one side of via della Conciliazione and piazza Pio XII; Italian Wikipedia records that its apse is still visible from Borgo Santo Spirito. It is the seat of the Centro Internazionale Giovanile San Lorenzo.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia dates the church to the twelfth century and notes a tradition ascribing it to Santa Galla in the sixth. The name in piscibus comes from the quarter's old name, Piscina, and possibly from a medieval fish market. When via della Conciliazione was cut the church was radically transformed and absorbed into the new frontage rather than demolished. It lies within the parish of Santa Maria in Traspontina and carries a cardinal-deacon's title.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria Annunziata in Borgo (l'Annunziatina)
places.summary: A small oratory on Lungotevere Vaticano, built 1742–1745 by Pietro Passalacqua as the oratory of the Archconfraternity of the Santo Spirito hospital.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia records that it was built on Borgo Santo Spirito, dismantled in 1940 for via della Conciliazione and re-erected ten years later on its present site by the Tiber. It holds works rescued from the demolished church of San Michele Arcangelo ai Corridori, among them a Madonna del latte attributed to Antoniazzo Romano.

places.name: Chiesa dei Santi Michele e Magno
places.summary: A church of the first half of the twelfth century at the top of a steep flight of steps off largo degli Alicorni, with a Romanesque bell tower and a Baroque interior. Italian Wikipedia gives it as the national church of the Frisians, today serving Rome's Dutch Catholic community and the Archconfraternity of the Blessed Sacrament in St Peter's.
places.history: Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership of this property (Art. 13; Annex II). Art. 15 states that the property, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is on Italian soil and visitors are subject to Italian law. The Holy See's enumeration names the «Chiesa dei Ss. Michele e Magno» among the properties on the Janiculum that hold that status. Italian Wikipedia dates the consecration to 30 January 1141 and records an eighteenth-century rebuilding by Carlo Murena; its dates for that rebuilding and for the reconsecration contradict one another within a single article, so none of them is given. The church was known in the Middle Ages as San Michele de Porticu and, from the fifteenth century, as San Michele in Borgo.

places.name: Chiesa di San Pietro in Borgo
places.summary: A medieval oratory on piazza del Sant'Uffizio, by Porta Cavalleggeri, restored as an oratory in 1923 within the Sant'Uffizio complex. Italian Wikipedia records fifteenth-century frescoes, a sixteenth-century Madonna col Bambino, and the burial of cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia describes the oratory as standing on Italian soil subject to extraterritoriality in favour of the Holy See; the Holy See's own enumeration names the Palazzo del Sant'Offizio «ed adiacenze» and does not itemise the oratory. On the building itself the same article gives an eleventh-century origin, records the church also as San Salvatore de ossibus and in terrione, and lists it among the Vatican basilica's dependencies in papal bulls of 1053, 1158 and 1186; the Schola Francorum hospice adjoined it. It was restored under Nicholas V, then abandoned and partly destroyed for the building of the Palazzo del Sant'Uffizio.

places.name: Cappella di Santa Monica
places.summary: The chapel of the Augustinians' Collegio Internazionale S. Monica, on piazza del Sant'Uffizio facing San Pietro in Borgo, built in 1941 by Giuseppe Momo. Italian Wikipedia records that it has been a cardinal-deaconry since 30 September 2023.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia describes it as the chapel of the Collegio Internazionale degli Agostiniani, beside their curia generalizia. The Holy See's own published enumeration names the Collegio Internazionale S. Monica among the properties on the Janiculum that hold extraterritorial status. Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership of this property (Art. 13; Annex II). Art. 15 states that the property, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is on Italian soil and visitors are subject to Italian law. The enumeration does not address the chapel individually.

places.name: Cappella di San Francesco Borgia
places.summary: A chapel inside the Jesuit Curia Generalizia at Borgo Santo Spirito 4.
places.history: The Cappella di San Francesco Borgia stands inside the Jesuit Curia Generalizia at Borgo Santo Spirito 4. The Holy See's own published enumeration of its extraterritorial properties names the Curia Generalizia della Compagnia di Gesù, and separately the buildings on Borgo Santo Spirito adjoining it, among the properties on the Janiculum that hold extraterritorial status. Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership of this property (Art. 13; Annex II). Art. 15 states that the property, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is on Italian soil and visitors are subject to Italian law. The enumeration does not address the chapel individually.

places.name: Palazzo del Sant'Uffizio
places.summary: A palace first built in 1514 for cardinal Lorenzo Pucci and bought by Pius V in 1566 or 1567 for 9,000 scudi to house the Inquisition. Italian Wikipedia gives it today as the seat of the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and other Curia offices.
places.history: Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership of this property (Art. 13; Annex II). Art. 15 states that the property, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is on Italian soil and visitors are subject to Italian law. The Holy See's enumeration names «il Palazzo del Sant'Offizio ed adiacenze, sede della Congregazione della Dottrina della Fede». Italian Wikipedia records that the façade was rebuilt in 1524–1525 by Giuliano Leni, Pietro Roselli and Michelangelo, that Antonio da Sangallo il Giovane continued the work from 1532, that Pirro Ligorio and Giovanni Sallustio Peruzzi carried out restorations, and that Sixtus V built prisons there in 1586. The same article contains an impossible sentence, dating a restoration by Leo XII to 1811–1814 when Leo XII reigned from 1823; it is not repeated here.

places.name: Pontificio Istituto Patristico Augustinianum
places.summary: A pontifical institute for the study of the Fathers of the Church, with the Biblioteca Augustinianum and a congress centre comprising the Auditorium «p. Agostino Trapè», an Aula Minor and other rooms. Its own site gives the address as Via Paolo VI 25 and the telephone as +39 06 68006238.
places.history: Everything above comes from the institute's own site, which describes itself in those terms and posts its own academic calendar. The institute is not named anywhere in the Holy See's published enumeration of its extraterritorial properties, and no such status is claimed for it here.

places.name: Porta Santo Spirito
places.summary: A gate on via di Porta Santo Spirito, behind the hospital, rebuilt in the mid-sixteenth century by Antonio da Sangallo il Giovane for Paul III after the Sack of 1527. Roma Capitale records that it was left unfinished and remains so.
places.history: Roma Capitale's tourism office states that the gate stands on what was the southern limit of the Civitas Leonina, walled by Leo IV around 850, and that Sangallo rebuilt it for Paul III after the Landsknechte of Charles V sacked Rome in 1527. Bastions were added around it by Pius IV in 1564. It has a large central archway flanked by pairs of Doric columns and niches. In 1642, under Urban VIII, the building of the Mura Gianicolensi enclosed the gate inside a new circuit and it lost its function. Italian Wikipedia adds the earlier name posterula Saxonum and a renaming under Innocent III. This is also the Roma Capitale page that gets the 1527 Sack right, against its own Castel Sant'Angelo page.

places.name: Porta Castello
places.summary: A vanished gate, and a name commonly attached to the wrong object. What visitors photograph at the corner of via di Porta Castello and Borgo Sant'Angelo is not the gate: Italian Wikipedia records it as a pair of arches cut through the wall of the Passetto for traffic, one by Pius IV and one by the Comune di Roma.
places.history: The gate itself stood in the stretch of wall Pius IV added to the Civitas Leonina around 1563, at what is now the junction of via di Porta Castello, via delle Fosse di Castello and via Giovanni Vitelleschi. It was closed in 1798, and the wall from piazza Risorgimento to Castel Sant'Angelo, with both its gates, was demolished in the late-nineteenth-century works. Italian Wikipedia records that it was probably twin to Porta Angelica, carrying the same Pius IV arms and inscriptions — Piale, writing in 1828, recorded «PIUS IIII. PONT. MAX. PORTAM NOVAM ET MOENIA A FUNDAMENTIS EREXIT» on both — and that Cola di Rienzo entered Rome in triumph through it on 1 August 1354.

places.name: Galleria Principe Amedeo di Savoia-Aosta
places.summary: A road tunnel under the Janiculum, running between Porta Cavalleggeri and Porta Santo Spirito. Its Porta Santo Spirito portal is in Borgo; the far portal is outside the rione, in Quartiere XIII Aurelio.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia credits the design to Cesare Bazzani from 1930, dates the works from 1938 and the opening to 1940, and gives a single bore of 0.250 km, 16 metres in diameter. The tunnel was originally called the galleria Gianicolense. Motorcycles under 125 cc are excluded from it.

places.name: Borgo Pio
places.summary: One of the three streets Pius IV laid out from 1565, running from via di Porta Castello to via di Porta Angelica. It is also called borgo Sant'Anna.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia, citing Rendina and Paradisi, records that the street was established by Pius IV's bull «Erectionis civitatis Piae prope arcem Sancti Angeli» of 5 December 1565, and that construction continued under Gregory XIII, attested by an epigraph dated anno VIII MDLXXX. Borgo Pio, Borgo Vittorio and Borgo Angelico were laid out together from 1565 as the Civitas Pia: Borgo Vittorio takes its name from the victory at Lepanto, Borgo Angelico from Angelo, Pius IV's baptismal name.

places.name: Borgo Santo Spirito
places.summary: A medieval street running from via San Pio X to largo degli Alicorni, paved in sampietrini, along the front of the Santo Spirito hospital complex.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia records its earlier names — Burgus Saxonum, Burgus Frisonum, Borgo San Michele, Borgo San Martino — and that until 1870 the stretch of today's via dei Penitenzieri between numbers 12 and 32 formed part of it.

entries.name: Castel Sant'Angelo
entries.note: Hadrian's mausoleum, later a fortress and a papal refuge, a museum site since 1925 and open Tuesday to Sunday 9.00–19.30, last admission 18.30.

entries.name: Via della Conciliazione
entries.note: About 420 metres of sampietrini between two rows of obelisk lampposts, cut from 1936 across the demolished spina and completed for the Jubilee of 1950.

entries.name: Passetto di Borgo
entries.note: The fortified corridor formed in 1277 under Nicholas III, used as an escape route by Alexander VI in 1494 and Clement VII in 1527.

entries.name: Arcispedale di Santo Spirito in Saxia
entries.note: Made a hospital by Innocent III in 1198 on the site of the Schola Saxonum; the Corsia Sistina built for Sixtus IV runs 120 metres by 12 under an octagonal tiburio.

entries.name: Palazzo del Commendatore
entries.note: Built 1566–1572 under Pius V; only the arcaded courtyard is visitable, Monday to Friday 7.30–18.00 and Saturday 7.30–12.00, and it holds a six-hour clock whose single hand is shaped like a lizard.

entries.name: Museo storico nazionale dell'arte sanitaria
entries.note: Opened in 1933 inside the hospital complex, with wax models in the sala Flajani and Paolo Mascagni's anatomical plates; no source states its hours.

entries.name: Chiesa di Santo Spirito in Sassia (Santuario della Divina Misericordia)
entries.note: Built 1538–1590 and consecrated on 17 May 1571, with a bell tower of about 1471–1475 given to Baccio Pontelli.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Maria in Traspontina
entries.note: The Carmelite parish church, its dome kept flat and drumless to clear the field of fire of Castel Sant'Angelo's guns; visitor entrance at via della Conciliazione 14.

entries.name: Palazzo dei Penitenzieri (Palazzo della Rovere)
entries.note: Begun about 1480 for cardinal Domenico Della Rovere; the right wing, holding Pinturicchio's Soffitto dei Semidei of 1490, is visitable on request to the Equestrian Order.

entries.name: Palazzo Castellesi (Giraud, Torlonia)
entries.note: Built 1499–1517 for cardinal Adriano Castellesi and faced piazza Scossacavalli until the spina came down; a private residence now, so the façade is what you see.

entries.name: Porta Santo Spirito
entries.note: Rebuilt by Antonio da Sangallo il Giovane for Paul III after the Sack of 1527 and left unfinished; the Mura Gianicolensi of 1642 enclosed it and it lost its function.

entries.name: Borgo Pio
entries.note: Laid out from 1565 under Pius IV's bull of 5 December, running from via di Porta Castello to via di Porta Angelica.

entries.name: Borgo Santo Spirito
entries.note: A medieval street in sampietrini along the front of the hospital, known in turn as Burgus Saxonum, Burgus Frisonum, Borgo San Michele and Borgo San Martino.

links.note: The Bambino Gesù hospital and Sant'Onofrio al Gianicolo are on the Holy See's extraterritorial list, but they stand in Trastevere, not Borgo.
Santa Maria Maggiore, in Monti, is a Lateran Treaty extraterritorial property of the same third tier as Borgo's Holy See palaces.
Campitelli, across the Tiber, holds the Roman Forum, the Palatine and the Capitoline Museums.
A three-day Rome itinerary that takes in the Vatican and lunch in Borgo's side streets.
